body:
## Summary

- adds the versioned cross-VM collection identity protocol for EVM and Solana
- defines stable normalized deployment and logical collection digests
- binds finality policy into candidate, work, evidence, cache, and report inputs
- adds capability-registry epoch/sequence semantics and strict Effect boundary schemas
- publishes positive, malformed, digest, Dashboard-shaped, and Sonar-shaped fixtures

## Verification

- `pnpm typecheck`
- `pnpm test` — 22 tests
- `pnpm clean && pnpm build`
- independent Fable review: PASS
- independent SHA-256/JCS vector reproduction

## Coordination

- Task: CR-001
- Coordinator epic: `collection-report-coordinator-f09`
- Aggregate issue: #472

This PR is intentionally draft. It must not be merged until the coordinated collection-report gates permit it.

## Summary
Verdict: COMMENT. This PR has the right architectural instinct: define identity as a canonical protocol surface, then defend it with fixtures and consumer tests. The main concerns are narrow but important: exported helpers should protect runtime callers with the same rigor as schema boundaries, and digest integrity checks should stay whole-object by habit.

The larger pattern here is protocol durability. Cross-VM identity will outlive today’s TypeScript types, so every public helper is part of the wire contract, not just convenience code.

## Findings
<!-- bridge-findings-start -->

JavaScript callers or TypeScript callers using unchecked values can produce digests whose domain or major_version fail the exported VersionedDigest schema.",
      "suggestion": "Decode the inputs with DigestDomain and an integer >= 1 schema before canonicalizing, or return a typed validation error when domain/majorVersion are invalid.",
      "faang_parallel": "Google’s Protocol Buffers practice treats generated types as helpful, but still validates at service boundaries because wire data and runtime callers can bypass compile-time guarantees.",
      "metaphor": "This is like printing an official passport without checking the date of birth field first; the seal looks real, but the document may not pass the next border.",
      "teachable_moment": "In protocol packages, exported helpers are boundary APIs. If they mint branded values, they should either validate or make invalid construction impossible.",
      "connection": "This connects to the broader schema-vs-runtime gap: TypeScript narrows authoring mistakes, but published packages still serve JavaScript, tests, migrations, and future agents.",

## Callouts
[Test Coverage] The malformed fixture suite is unusually strong for a first protocol slice. It teaches future contributors what must be rejected, which is often more valuable than showing only valid examples.

[Quality] The separation across `canonical`, `contracts`, `registry-version`, and `scalars` gives the protocol a readable shape. That modularity will matter when other VMs or registry versions arrive.

[Operational] Consumer tests for dashboard and sonar are a good signal: this PR is not just defining an abstract schema, it is checking that real downstream shapes can depend on it.

## Summary

Verdict: `REQUEST_CHANGES`. The protocol shape is strong: digest integrity checks and decimal-string registry sequences show disciplined boundary design. The two medium issues are both hash-boundary problems, and they deserve tightening before this becomes a cross-VM identity contract.

Canonical protocols live or die at the boundary between “typed in memory” and “valid on the wire.” The broad lesson here is the same one behind systems like Bigtable, Borg, and Tink: canonical forms must be narrower than application objects, and digest domains must be explicit enough that a valid hash cannot mean the wrong thing.

[Test Coverage] The malformed fixture suite is doing real work here. It turns edge cases into executable doctrine, which is how future maintainers learn the contract without guessing.

## Summary
Verdict: `REQUEST_CHANGES`. The protocol shape is strong: strict boundary decoding and digest recomputation show real care for cross-VM identity. The main concern is correctness at the contract edge: one test appears to assert Solana case behavior with an invalid base58 key, and packaging expectations for fixtures should be made explicit before this becomes a downstream dependency.

The architectural through-line here is identity determinism. Cross-VM protocols succeed when every consumer can independently arrive at the same bytes, the same digest, and the same rejection reasons.
